div.p: THE MORTALITY OF RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

THE twin towns of Runcorn and Widnes-1 Lancashire and Cheshire joining hands over the tidal wave which ebbs and flows between them— may well feel a keen interest in the story issued periodically by the Registrar General, and which, if it does not tell the , world how the inhabitants live, explains how I and why it is that they die. The authori- ties of these towns on the Mersey have com- mitted to their keeping important duties which one is willing to believe they are zeal- 1 ens to perform, and yet in Runcorn at any I rate, the report we publish cannot be said to be a matter for congratulation. The Runcorn Commisaionere have yet evidently , much to accomplish before that ancient ' town, once famed an a salubrious resort for unfeebled invalids. can invite comparison with its old and well-merited reputation. In ' the deaths of children the figures are indeed staggering, and seem to suggest that a very Herod of malaria is ravaging that hapless community. Stringent inquiry should be instituted into the causes of this extraordin- ary infant mortality and measures should be promptly taken to stay the plague amongst the" innocents" of Runcorn. The children in Widnes seem to be equally plague- ' stricken, the mortality there 'being for the • past quarter "unusually heavy." We may be well justified in urging this matter on the attention of those who are appointed as pro- teeters of the public: health in these towns. ' A great moral and official responsibility will be exacted by public opinion if all is not done that can be done to mitigate the state of things described as follows:— The report of the Registrar General on the health of Runcorn in the December quarter of 1878, shows that there is nn im- provement in the health of the town. The deaths were then greatly in excess of the average, and the present return shows the same thing. When it is seen that the deaths in a town in two consecutive quarters show • considerable increase, to say the least, it must be a matter for regret and a subject worthy of the immediate attend ai of the sanitary authorities. this is especially so in Runcorn, for in the last quarter there were prevalent several of the principal symotio diseases which alone carried off IS. Small-pox is credited with two desks, scarlet fever 3, and fever 3. With such destructive elements in Runcorn, it is to be feared that in the current quarter they may carry off • still greater number. During last quarter they were RIO births in Runcorn, Watt's, and Halton, and the fact of there having been only 190 in the same three months of 1875 shows the gradual increase in the population. The ge of the corresponding periods of 1879-4 5 lead us to expect 99 deaths, but there were as many as 114, showing a lose of 15 lives. No doubt that the increase in the deaths is due to some extent to the growth of the popula- tion, but more, however, to the prevalence of the principal xymotic diseases. Small-pox was fatal in September in two cases, and again there were two more in the succeeding three months. 'there was a fresh outbreak of scarlet fever which carried off three. Of the 114 death. in Runcorn as many as 36 were those of infants undo: one year. Bad as this is, it is, however, an improvement in the September return when there were CI Here then Runcorn in six months had 82 I deaths of children under one year. This ie a deplorable loss of infantile life, and it is diffie cult to account for so great a sacrifice. It represents nearly a third of the whole deaths in Runcorn. There were live deaths due here to violence, and inquests were held on nine bodies in the last quarter. Budworth, Stretton, Hale, and Appleton send a favourable report, as there were only 117 deaths, being 6 below the average. An equally good return is sent by Daresbury, Hatton, Preston, and Dutton, where there were only 18 deaths. and 12 of these referred to persons who had attained the age of 60 years and upwards. In Frodsham, Hobby, Kingsley, and Norley, there were 89 births, end the 32 deaths were below the average' by 3. T. are was a fresh outbreak of scarlet fever here, which proved fatal in two cases. 1 It is evident from the late reports from , rrescot that there has been going on a gradual diminution in the mortality of the town, and seeing, too, that in the present report the deaths from the principal symotic diming.a were fewer, we may safely say that the health of the town compares favourably with the healthiest of like centres of popula- tion. The present report shows there were 92 deaths in rresoot in the December quar- ter, and the average gives 6 more. Out of these 92 deaths, 08 many as 21 were those of elderly people. Smallpox was again fatal in one case, and fever was credited with 7 deaths, there being only one in September period. Ihe births in Prescot numbered 141. The were 24 deaths in the quarter in the Workhouse. The mortality in Rale, Spoke, and Hale- wood more than doubled the average, being 21. No fewer, however, than 8 of these were due to violence. Much Woolton had 45 births, and the 34 deaths were in excese In Iluyton, Tarbock, and Knowsley there were 45 births and 10 deaths. The town of Widnes is so rapidly increas- ing that it would be matter for local public interest if it were formed into a registration distriot of its own. As it is, it is impossible to state how many births or deaths takes place in that tow nchip, and we are helpless to find out the causes of death most preva- lent. It is placed in the sub-district of Fernworth, so the figures refer to all the other places included in it. These are Widnes, Far nworth, Cronton, and Di•ton. In the last quarter there were 254 births, and as there were 121 deaths, they repro- eent the exact average for the quarter. This shows a decrease of 10 on the September quarter. There was an unusually heavy mortality in Widnes, An, among children, as 40 deaths were those of infants under one year. There is a slight decline in the viru- lence of scarlet fever, there being 10 deaths against 13 in September. Fever was credited with 5. The deaths from violence gradually show an increase, as the present return gives 11, and inquests were held on 15 bodies. In St. Helens, Sutton, rare and Windle there were 582 births, and as there were only 275 deaths, they were as many as 108 below the number expected. Such a fact speak volumes for the improved condition of these districts.
